signals.title: [Bug] Databricks provider drops Anthropic prompt-cache token counts when streaming
signals.text: **LiteLLM version:** v1.96.0 (also reproduced on v1.90.2) **Provider:** `databricks` (Azure Databricks Foundation Model API, Claude models) **Model:** `system.ai.claude-opus-5` ## What happens With `stream: false`, prompt-cache token counts are returned correctly. With `stream: true`, `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` are absent from the usage object entirely — not zero, absent. Because spend is computed from the usage object, every streamed Databricks request is costed at the full input rate even when it was served from cache. For an Anthropic-format agent client that always streams and relies on prompt caching, this makes reported spend diverge sharply from actual provider cost. Importantly, **caching itself works** — only the accounting is broken. See "Caching is actually working" below. ## Reproduction Identical payload, only `stream` differs. Fallbacks and retries disabled. ```python body = { "model": "claude-opus", # -> databricks/system.ai.claude-opus-5 "max_tokens": 8, "system": [{"type": "text", "text": CORPUS, # ~9.6k tokens "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}], "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with OK."}], "disable_fallbacks": True, "num_retries": 0, } ``` **Non-streaming — correct:** ``` 1st (cold) input_tokens=11 cache_creation_input_tokens=9603 cache_read_input_tokens=None 2nd (warm) input_tokens=11 cache_creation_input_tokens=None cache_read_input_tokens=9603 ``` **Streaming — cache fields missing from every event:** ``` message_start usage: {"input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": ...} message_delta usage: {"input_tokens": 11, "output_tokens": 1} ``` ### Same-endpoint control, with `stream_options` To rule out `stream_options` as the cause, the following ran against `/v1/chat/completions` with `"stream_options": {"include_usage": true}` on both providers — identical payload, identical proxy, only the provider differs: ``` anthropic cold prompt_tokens_details: {"cached_tokens": 0, "text_tokens": 10, "cache_write_tokens": ...} anthropic warm prompt_tokens_details: {"cached_tokens": 13304, "text_tokens": 10, "cache_write_tokens": ...} databricks cold (no prompt_tokens_details) prompt_tokens: 7015 databricks warm (no prompt_tokens_details) prompt_tokens: 7015 ``` The Anthropic provider is correct in both streaming and non-streaming modes. Note also that **without** `stream_options: {"include_usage": true}` the Databricks streaming response contains **no usage chunk at all**. Setting `general_settings.always_include_stream_usage: true` restores the usage chunk but still yields no cache fields — so the gap is in response parsing, not in the request or in `stream_options` handling. ## Caching is actually working A streamed request with `cache_control` was sent, then the same corpus was sent non-streaming. The non-streaming call reported `cached_tokens: 13303` on its *first* call — i.e. the preceding streaming request had populated the cache. So streaming requests participate in caching normally; the tokens are simply never surfaced in the usage object. This means reported cost for streamed Databricks traffic is inflated relative to the provider's actual metering. ## Cause In `litellm/llms/databricks/chat/transformation.py`: - **Line 643** (non-streaming) works only incidentally: ```python setattr(model_response, "usage", Usage(**completion_response["usage"])) ``` The provider's whole `usage` dict is splatted into `Usage`, so cache keys survive because they happen to be present — not because they are handled. - **Line 665**, `class DatabricksChatResponseIterator(BaseModelResponseIterator)`, has no equivalent. Grepping the entire `litellm/llms/databricks/` tree returns **zero** matches for `cache_creation`, `cache_read`, or `cached_tokens`, whereas `litellm/llms/anthropic/chat/transformation.py` handles them explicitly. `DatabricksConfig` inherits from `AnthropicConfig` (`class DatabricksConfig(DatabricksBase, OpenAILikeChatConfig, AnthropicConfig)`, line 152), but the streaming response iterator is a separate class that does not inherit Anthropic's usage parsing. ## Expected `DatabricksChatResponseIterator` should extract `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` from streaming chunks and populate `usage.prompt_tokens_details`, matching both the Anthropic provider and the Databricks non-streaming path. ## Impact Spend tracking is wrong for any streaming Databricks request that uses prompt caching — which is every request from an Anthropic-format agent client. Cache-aware pricing (`cache_read_input_token_cost`, `cache_creation_input_token_cost`) is configured on the deployment and applied correctly on the Anthropic provider, but cannot take effect here because the token counts never reach the cost calculator. ## Related Separate bug in the same provider, filed as #36931 — the Databricks request path emits LiteLLM's internal `thinking_blocks` field instead of Databricks' documented `reasoning` content block, breaking multi-turn extended thinking. Independent of this issue.
signals.author: pokepoke81

signals.title: [Bug]: /model/info pricing metadata becomes worker-dependent after successful requests in v1.98.0
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I searched the open and closed issues before filing this report The closest result I found was [#30484](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/30484), which mentions a completed team-scoped `/v1/model/info` consistency item. This report is a different failure mode: pricing fields in `/model/info` change according to the Uvicorn worker handling the request after successful model traffic, even without team filtering ### What happened? After upgrading a live LiteLLM proxy from v1.96.0 to v1.98.0, repeated authenticated requests to `GET /model/info` stopped returning a stable model catalog For the same caller, key, URL, configuration, and database state, one response contains built-in pricing fields while another response omits those fields for a different subset of models. In a 12-request sample, I observed seven distinct canonicalized pricing variants. The number of rows missing at least one checked pricing field ranged from 12 to 40 The behavior is process-local: - A direct connection to a mature pod exposes two stable variants, matching its two Uvicorn workers - Different pods converge on different affected subsets based on the successful requests handled by each process - A fresh worker initially returns the expected pricing metadata - Successful model requests cause the affected entries to lose pricing metadata in that worker - Restarting workers clears the symptom temporarily, but it returns after normal traffic - The public raw model cost map still contains the correct prices on the same affected worker This does not appear to be a Redis race. The corruption reproduces in one Python process with no Redis or database, and the object being changed is returned by a process-local `functools.lru_cache`. Redis and the load balancer make the production symptom easier to notice, but neither is needed to trigger it The affected fields are: - `input_cost_per_token` - `output_cost_per_token` - `input_cost_per_character` - `output_cost_per_character` - `cache_read_input_token_cost` - `cache_creation_input_token_cost` Because `/model/info` strips `None` values before serializing the response, the corrupted fields are omitted rather than returned as explicit nulls ### User Flow Before a hypothetical fix: 1. Send an authenticated `GET /model/info` request to display the available model catalog 2. Send successful chat completion requests through the same proxy 3. Repeat the authenticated `GET /model/info` request 4. Read pricing metadata that is present or absent depending on which worker served the catalog request After a hypothetical fix: 1. Send an authenticated `GET /model/info` request to display the available model catalog 2. Send successful chat completion requests through the same proxy 3. Repeat the authenticated `GET /model/info` request 4. Read the same pricing metadata from every response regardless of which worker served the catalog request ### Proof the bug occurs #### Live end-to-end setup The production identifiers below are deliberately replaced. The observed topology and behavior are unchanged: - Multiple Kubernetes replicas behind one HTTP load balancer - Two Uvicorn workers per replica - PostgreSQL-backed model configuration with `store_model_in_db` enabled - Redis enabled for shared proxy features - Real provider requests, not mocked responses - LiteLLM v1.98.0 - Previous working version v1.96.0 Sanitized configuration: ```yaml general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL store_model_in_db: true ``` Sanitized start command: ```bash litellm --config /app/config.yaml --port 4000 --num_workers 2 ``` Environment variable names used by the reproduction: ```bash export PROXY_URL="https://proxy.example.com" export LITELLM_KEY="<redacted>" ``` A successful request to a real configured deployment was used to exercise the normal success callback: ```bash curl -sS "$PROXY_URL/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "model-a", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with OK"}], "max_tokens": 4 }' | jq '{ request_succeeded: (.choices | length > 0), finish_reason: .choices[0].finish_reason }' ``` Output: ```json { "request_succeeded": true, "finish_reason": "stop" } ``` The following samples only model names and three pricing fields, canonicalizes the result, and prints aggregate values so no deployment names or response data are disclosed: ```bash sample_dir="$(mktemp -d)" for i in $(seq 1 12); do curl -sS "$PROXY_URL/model/info" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \ > "$sample_dir/$i.json" done python3 - "$sample_dir" <<'PY' import hashlib import json import pathlib import sys directory = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]) files = sorted(directory.glob("*.json")) fields = ( "input_cost_per_token", "output_cost_per_token", "cache_read_input_token_cost", ) digests = set() missing_counts = [] for path in files: rows = json.loads(path.read_text())["data"] projection = [] missing = 0 for row in rows: info = row.get("model_info") or {} projection.append( { "model_name": row.get("model_name"), **{field: info.get(field) for field in fields}, } ) if any(info.get(field) is None for field in fields): missing += 1 projection.sort(key=lambda item: str(item["model_name"])) encoded = json.dumps( projection, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ).encode() digests.add(hashlib.sha256(encoded).hexdigest()) missing_counts.append(missing) print(f"samples={len(files)}") print(f"unique_pricing_variants={len(digests)}") print(f"missing_pricing_rows_min={min(missing_counts)}") print(f"missing_pricing_rows_max={max(missing_counts)}") PY ``` Output from the live v1.98.0 proxy: ```text samples=12 unique_pricing_variants=7 missing_pricing_rows_min=12 missing_pricing_rows_max=40 ``` A persistent connection pinned to one worker and a persistent connection pinned to the other worker returned the following representative row. The model identifier was replaced one-for-one, and numeric values were reduced to presence booleans: ```text worker_a_model_info={"model_name":"model-a","input_cost_per_token_present":true,"output_cost_per_token_present":true,"cache_read_input_token_cost_present":true} worker_b_model_info={"model_name":"model-a","input_cost_per_token_present":false,"output_cost_per_token_present":false,"cache_read_input_token_cost_present":false} worker_b_raw_cost_map={"model_name":"provider/model-a","input_cost_per_token_present":true,"output_cost_per_token_present":true,"cache_read_input_token_cost_present":true} ``` This shows that the source cost map is intact while the derived cached model info is corrupted inside one worker #### Deterministic single-process reproduction This reproduction uses the v1.98.0 package, no HTTP server, no Redis, no database, no mocks, and no provider credentials. It selects a public cost-map entry with three populated pricing fields without printing the model name: ```python import copy import litellm from litellm import Router from litellm.types.router import Deployment, LiteLLM_Params, ModelInfo FIELDS = ( "input_cost_per_token", "output_cost_per_token", "cache_read_input_token_cost", ) model_info_name, cost_entry = next( (name, info) for name, info in litellm.model_cost.items() if "/" in name and info.get("litellm_provider") == name.split("/", 1)[0] and all(info.get(field) is not None for field in FIELDS) ) provider, provider_model = model_info_name.split("/", 1) litellm.get_model_info.cache_clear() before = copy.deepcopy(litellm.get_model_info(model=model_info_name)) deployment = Deployment( model_name="cache-repro", litellm_params=LiteLLM_Params( model=provider_model, custom_llm_provider=provider, ), model_info=ModelInfo(id="cache-repro"), ) router = Router() router.get_router_model_info( deployment=deployment, received_model_name="cache-repro", ) after = litellm.get_model_info(model=model_info_name) raw = litellm.model_cost[model_info_name] def present(info): return tuple(info.get(field) is not None for field in FIELDS) print("before_present=", present(before)) print("after_present=", present(after)) print("raw_map_present=", present(raw)) print( "same_cached_object=", after is litellm.get_model_info(model=model_info_name), ) ``` Output on v1.98.0: ```text before_present= (True, True, True) after_present= (False, False, False) raw_map_present= (True, True, True) same_cached_object= True ``` Clearing `litellm.get_model_info`'s cache restores the values until the same merge path runs again. Passing an equivalent plain dictionary with absent pricing keys does not erase the values, which isolates the trigger to the Pydantic deployment path with unset fields ### Root cause The regression begins with [4de7a7443a](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/4de7a7443ac5506f422efb36e96387aaae185607), merged by [d0758a291c](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/d0758a291c9dd5405dd8310fd02bccdd5b8b87ff) in PR #36215 That change makes router `ModelInfo` inherit `MirroredPricingParams`, which declares the six pricing fields with defaults of `None`: ```python class MirroredPricingParams(BaseModel): input_cost_per_token: float | None = None output_cost_per_token: float | None = None input_cost_per_character: float | None = None output_cost_per_character: float | None = None cache_read_input_token_cost: float | None = None cache_creation_input_token_cost: float | None = None ``` The existing router merge obtains an object from `litellm.get_model_info()` and mutates it in place: ```python model_info = litellm.get_model_info(model=model_info_name) user_model_info = deployment.get("model_info") or {} if model_info is not None: model_info.update(cast(ModelInfo, user_model_info)) return model_info ``` At the same time, `litellm.get_model_info()` returns the object held by an LRU cache: ```python @lru_cache(maxsize=DEFAULT_MAX_LRU_CACHE_SIZE) def _cached_get_model_info(...): return _build_model_info(...) ``` The failure sequence is: 1. `litellm.get_model_info()` returns a mutable cached object containing valid built-in prices 2. A successful request invokes `Router.deployment_callback_on_success()` 3. The callback reaches `get_router_model_info()` with a Pydantic `Deployment` 4. Iterating the nested Pydantic `ModelInfo` includes the newly declared pricing fields even when they were never configured 5. `dict.update()` writes those `None` defaults over the valid prices in the cached object 6. Later `get_model_info()` calls in the same process return the already-mutated object 7. `/model/info` strips the `None` values, so the fields disappear from JSON 8. Each worker corrupts only the entries touched by requests routed through that process, producing worker-dependent responses The same in-place update existed in v1.96.0, but router `ModelInfo` did not yet declare these mirrored pricing fields. Unset values therefore were not present during model iteration and did not overwrite the cached built-in values ### Suggested fix The merge should both avoid mutating an object owned by the LRU cache and exclude unset or `None` Pydantic defaults: ```python cached_model_info = litellm.get_model_info(model=model_info_name) raw_user_model_info = deployment.get("model_info") or {} if isinstance(raw_user_model_info, BaseModel): user_model_info = raw_user_model_info.model_dump(exclude_none=True) else: user_model_info = { key: value for key, value in raw_user_model_info.items() if value is not None } return { **cached_model_info, **user_model_info, } ``` This preserves explicit non-null deployment overrides, keeps built-in prices when the deployment did not provide an override, and returns a fresh dictionary rather than modifying shared cached state Suggested regression coverage: 1. A Pydantic `Deployment` with unset pricing fields must not change the object returned by later `litellm.get_model_info()` calls 2. Unset pricing fields must preserve built-in prices 3. Explicit non-null pricing overrides must still win 4. Dictionary and Pydantic deployment paths must produce equivalent merged metadata 5. Running the success callback must not change a later `/model/info` response 6. Two routers or workers processing different model subsets must still expose identical pricing metadata A fix with regression tests has been validated locally and can be submitted as a PR ### Related independent reload finding During diagnosis I also found a separate v1.98.0 DB-only reload edge case. It does not cause the `None` overwrite above, but it can add another source of model-cost-map inconsistency around startup or manual reloads The schedule work in [9ea5cfce0e](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/9ea5cfce0edd365f722556d3d72960f1d60012ac) can cause a newly started process to perform a one-time model cost map swap when a persisted manual reload revision exists. A DB-only proxy constructs `Router()` before loading deployments, and router tracking currently depends on a truthy initial `model_list`. That router is therefore absent from `_live_routers`, so `reapply_runtime_model_cost_registrations()` cannot replay the dynamically loaded DB deployments after the swap Registering every live Router, including an initially empty Router that is populated later, fixes that replay gap. I included this note to distinguish it from the primary cache-mutation regression and am happy to file it separately if maintainers prefer one root cause per issue ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.98.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: Admin UI session cookie is a non-HttpOnly JWT carrying the caller's proxy key
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? The Admin UI login sets a `token` cookie holding a JWT whose `key` claim is the caller's real proxy key, and the cookie is not marked `HttpOnly`. For a proxy admin signing in with `UI_USERNAME` / `UI_PASSWORD` or through SSO, that means a full-privilege `sk-...` key sits in `document.cookie`, readable by any script running on `/ui`, for the whole 8h cookie lifetime. Two things make it worse than a normal session cookie: The key keeps working outside the browser. Anything that can read the cookie can paste the decoded key into `curl` and mint new keys, read spend, or call models, with no session involved. Logout does not revoke it. The dashboard clears cookies client-side, so a key that was copied before logout stays valid until its own expiry. I would expect the browser to hold an opaque session identifier that the proxy resolves server-side, in an `HttpOnly` cookie, with a logout route that drops the session on the server. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Run the proxy with any config that sets a master key, for example ```yaml model_list: [] general_settings: master_key: sk-1234 ``` 2. Log in the way the Admin UI does, and look at the cookie it sets ``` $ curl -si -X POST http://localhost:4000/login -d 'username=admin&password=sk-1234' | grep -i '^set-cookie' set-cookie: token=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjoiZGVmYXVsdF91c2VyX2lkIiwia2V5Ijoic2steHh4eHh4...<truncated>; Path=/; SameSite=lax ``` No `HttpOnly` flag, so `document.cookie` in the devtools console on http://localhost:4000/ui/ returns the same string. 3. Decode the middle segment ``` $ echo "$TOKEN" | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d | python -m json.tool { "user_id": "default_user_id", "key": "sk-<the admin's real proxy key>", "user_role": "proxy_admin", "login_method": "username_password", "auth_header_name": "Authorization", "server_root_path": "", "exp": 1786805817 } ``` 4. Use that key from outside the browser ``` $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4000/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY_FROM_COOKIE" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"key_alias":"minted-outside-the-browser"}' { "key": "sk-...", "key_alias": "minted-outside-the-browser", "expires": null } ``` 5. Log out in the UI, then repeat step 4 with the same key; it still mints keys ### Relevant log output ```shell POST /login HTTP/1.1" 303 See Other POST /key/generate HTTP/1.1" 200 OK # using the key decoded out of the login cookie ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? UI Dashboard ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0 (reproduced on `litellm_internal_staging` at 423b791ee0) ### Possible direction I have a working change locally that swaps the JWT for an opaque `sso_<hex>` handle stored in the cache the `login_code` exchange already uses, delivered in an `HttpOnly` `SameSite=Lax` cookie, plus `/sso/session/me` for identity and `/sso/session/logout` for server-side revocation, with a credential-free `litellm_ui_session=1` marker so the dashboard can still tell a session exists. Happy to open a PR if that direction sounds right to you.

signals.title: GET /spend/logs has no pagination and OOM-kills the proxy on a large LiteLLM_SpendLogs
signals.text: ### What happens `GET /spend/logs` with no query parameters fetches every row of `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` into memory. On a table of ~110k rows (~371 MB on disk) this exhausts the container and the kernel kills it: ``` reason = OOMKilled exitCode = 137 limit = 4Gi ``` The proxy is unavailable for about a minute while it restarts. In our deployment that proxy fronts all model traffic, so a single admin API call takes every model in the cluster offline. Version: **v1.90.0**, PostgreSQL backend. ### Why it is not avoidable by the caller `view_spend_logs` accepts no pagination parameters at all — there is no `page`, `limit`, or `page_size` in the signature, only filters that all default to `None`: ```python async def view_spend_logs( api_key: Optional[str] = fastapi.Query(default=None, ...), user_id: Optional[str] = fastapi.Query(default=None, ...), request_id: Optional[str] = fastapi.Query(default=None, ...), start_date: Optional[str] = fastapi.Query(default=None, ...), end_date: Optional[str] = fastapi.Query(default=None, ...), summarize: bool = fastapi.Query(default=True, ...), ... ) ``` and the query is issued with no row cap: ```python data = await SpendLogsRepository(prisma_client).table.find_many( where=filter_query, order={...}, ) ``` `find_many` is called without `take`. A caller who passes no filters therefore cannot bound the result; the only way to stay safe is to know in advance not to call the endpoint. ### The paginated endpoints already exist `/spend/logs/v2` and `/spend/logs/ui` do the right thing: ```python page: int = fastapi.Query(default=1, ge=1) page_size: int = fastapi.Query(default=50, description="Number of items per page", ge=1, le=100) ``` and the admin UI calls those, not the legacy path. So the unbounded behaviour is isolated to the v1 endpoint — which is what makes this look like an oversight rather than a design choice. ### Suggested fix Any of these would close it; the first seems closest to existing behaviour: 1. Add `page` / `page_size` to `view_spend_logs` and pass `take`/`skip` through to `find_many`, mirroring the v2 endpoint. 2. Apply a server-side default cap (e.g. `take=1000`) when no `request_id` is given, and document that the endpoint truncates. 3. Deprecate `/spend/logs` in favour of `/spend/logs/v2` and have it return a `400` when called without filters, pointing at the paginated path. ### Reproducing Populate `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` with a few hundred thousand rows, set a container memory limit in the low gigabytes, then: ``` GET /spend/logs Authorization: Bearer <master key> ``` The request does not return; the connection closes when the process is killed. ### Notes - Retention does not fix this on its own. `maximum_spend_logs_retention_period` bounds growth over time, but a bursty workload can add tens of thousands of rows in a single day, so the table can cross the threshold within any retention window. - We mitigated locally by blocking the exact path at the ingress. That is possible only because the UI uses the `/ui` and `/v2` variants; it is a workaround for an operator, not a fix.

signals.title: Prisma engine watchdog treats ECHILD from waitpid as engine death and forces a reconnect
signals.text: ### The code `litellm/proxy/utils.py`, the thread that waits on the Prisma query engine: ```python def _waitpid_thread_func(self, pid, loop): """Note: uvloop/libuv may reap the child first via waitpid(-1, WNOHANG) in its SIGCHLD handler. In that case our waitpid raises ChildProcessError. we still notify the event loop because the engine is dead either way.""" try: os.waitpid(pid, 0) except ChildProcessError: pass except OSError: pass loop.call_soon_threadsafe(self._on_engine_death_from_thread, pid) ``` The comment states the reasoning: *"the engine is dead either way."* We think that is not true. `ChildProcessError` is `ECHILD`, which means **"no such child of mine"** — the child was reaped by someone else, or was never this process's child, or was reparented away. None of those implies the process exited. That distinction is load-bearing here, because this proxy really does have processes that are not its own children. In our container: ``` PID 1 litellm (the application) S PID 559 node-MainThread Z ← never reaped PID 1086 query-engine-de S ← PPID 1, reparented ``` The Node process Prisma spawns to bootstrap the engine exits at startup and stays a zombie for the pod's lifetime; the engine itself has been reparented. A `waitpid` against a PID that is alive but no longer the caller's child is exactly the case that raises `ECHILD`. ### The consequence The notification is unconditional, and the receiver does not re-check liveness: ```python def _on_engine_death_from_thread(self, dead_pid): if self._engine_confirmed_dead: return if dead_pid != self._engine_pid: return if self._consume_expected_death(dead_pid): return # ... engine_process_death + force reconnect ``` Three guards, none of which asks whether the process is running. The class already has `_is_engine_alive()` (`os.kill(pid, 0)`), and this path never calls it. So a spurious `ECHILD` and a real death produce byte-identical behaviour: a forced reconnect that tears down a working connection. ### What we observed, and what we did not establish We saw DB-backed admin endpoints (`/key/list`, `/spend/tags`, `/spend/logs`) intermittently return `500` alongside these log lines: ``` prisma-query-engine PID 4220 exited (waitpid thread); triggering reconnect. Attempting Prisma DB reconnect. reason=engine_process_death prisma-query-engine PID 0 is dead; reconnecting. ``` **We cannot say the incident we saw was a spurious `ECHILD`.** The pod was replaced before we could examine it, and our log retention did not cover that namespace at the time. On the replacement pod the endpoints have been stable and we have not reproduced it. We are reporting the code path rather than the incident: it is reachable, and on that path a live engine and a dead one are indistinguishable. The `PID 0 is dead` line is suggestive — `_is_engine_alive()` treats `_engine_pid <= 0` as alive, so a zeroed PID arriving on a death path looks anomalous — but we cannot tie it to either branch without the pod. ### Suggested fix One line, either way: - Call `_is_engine_alive(pid)` before notifying on the `ECHILD` path, **or** - Do not notify when `waitpid` *raised* — only when it *returned* a status. Related: `_reap_all_zombies()` is only invoked on engine-death paths, never periodically, which is why the startup zombie above survives for the life of the pod. Not a bug on its own, but it is why the process table looks the way it does. ### Version v1.90.0, PostgreSQL backend, container running the app as PID 1 with no init process.

signals.title: [Bug]: SCIM PATCH/PUT/DELETE /Users/{id} leave the in-memory user cache stale
signals.text: ## Problem The SCIM v2 user endpoints (`PATCH /scim/v2/Users/{id}`, `PUT /scim/v2/Users/{id}`, `DELETE /scim/v2/Users/{id}`) currently only write to `litellm_usertable` and do not refresh or invalidate the in-memory user cache used by `get_user_object` (which is keyed on the literal `user_id` per `auth_checks.py:1641`). The very next auth check that hits the cache serves the pre-mutation user, so: - `PUT` (full replace, e.g. an email or role change) does not take effect on auth until the management-object TTL expires. - `PATCH` (e.g. deactivation via `active: false`) does not take effect on auth until the TTL expires — even though the same PATCH has already called `_set_user_keys_blocked` to block the user's keys, the cached `LiteLLM_UserTable` still reports the user as active. - `DELETE` does not invalidate the cached `user_id` entry, so a same-user `POST /user/new` reusing the same ID would read a stale `user_email` / `metadata` / `teams` snapshot from the cache. ## Why this matters SCIM is the standard protocol for IdP-driven user sync (Okta, Azure AD, OneLogin, JumpCloud, etc.). Operators using an IdP-driven deployment expect a SCIM-driven deactivation or rename to take effect immediately on the proxy. Without cache invalidation, the stale read is silently served on every request for the TTL window — and in a multi-pod deployment, the window extends across replicas. This is the same multi-prefix cache Achilles heel pattern already fixed in: - #35565 (cycle 9): `/team/block` and `/team/unblock` - #36817 (cycle 12): SCIM `PATCH/PUT/DELETE /Groups/{id}` The `/Users` surface was missed in #36817 because the user cache key shape is different from the team cache key shape. The team cache is dual-keyed (`team_id:{id}` + `team_alias:{alias}`); the user cache is single-keyed on the literal `user_id`. Same defect class, different code path. ## Current behavior `PUT /scim/v2/Users/{id}` updates the DB row, returns the new SCIM user shape, and leaves `user_api_key_cache[user_id]` unchanged. ## Expected behavior `PUT` and `PATCH` should call `_refresh_cached_user(updated_user, ...)` after the database write. `DELETE` should invalidate the cache (not refresh, since the user no longer exists) by clearing both halves of the dual cache (local LRU + Redis) for the `user_id` key. `POST /scim/v2/Users` (`create_user`) needs no cache work — the user is new, not yet in cache. ## Proposed solution Add a `_refresh_cached_user` helper in `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py` (mirrors the existing `_refresh_cached_team` at `team_endpoints.py:153`). Import it into `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/scim/scim_v2.py` and call it from the 3 mutating endpoints. Pin with regression tests in `tests/test_litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/scim/test_scim_v2_endpoints.py` in a new `TestScimUserCacheInvalidation` class (mirrors cycle 12's `TestScimGroupCacheInvalidation`). ## Alternatives considered 1. Inline the cache write in each endpoint (no helper). Rejected: scatters cache-management knowledge across 3 endpoints, easy to miss on a future SCIM endpoint addition. 2. Reuse `_refresh_cached_team`. Rejected: cache key shape (`user_id` literal vs `team_id:{id}`) and model type (`LiteLLM_UserTable` vs `LiteLLM_TeamTableCachedObj`) differ. ## Scope One source file (`scim_v2.py`, ~25 lines), one helper file (`auth_checks.py`, ~15 lines), one test file (3 tests, ~250 lines). ## Acceptance criteria - `update_user` calls `_refresh_cached_user` exactly once with the post-mutation row. - `patch_user` calls `_refresh_cached_user` exactly once with the post-mutation row. - `delete_user` calls `user_api_key_cache.delete_cache(key=user_id)` AND `proxy_logging_obj.internal_usage_cache.dual_cache.async_delete_cache(key=user_id)` (gated on `proxy_logging_obj is not None`). - 3 new regression tests pass; each is verified to fail without the source fix. - Pre-existing SCIM test suite stays green. ## Backward compatibility No API surface change. Internal cache-management only. ## Risks - `_refresh_cached_user` is a new helper. If a future SCIM endpoint mutates `litellm_usertable` without calling it, the same defect recurs. Mitigation: cross-reference in the new issue body so future contributors see the pattern.
signals.author: Harsh23Kashyap

signals.title: [Bug]: Gemini TTS via /v1/audio/speech is never spend-tracked on the proxy (no spend log, key spend stays 0)
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? Gemini text-to-speech requests sent through the proxy's `POST /v1/audio/speech` return audio (200) but never show up in spend logs, never increment the virtual key's spend, and never count against budgets. OpenAI TTS through the same endpoint, same proxy, and same key is tracked fine, so this is specific to the Gemini path (and, by the same mechanism, any TTS provider that is served by translating the speech request into a chat completion under the hood) Expected: a `gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts` call priced at $0.30/M in and $2.50/M out shows a spend-log row with `call_type: aspeech` and non-zero `spend`, and the key's `spend` moves, exactly like `openai/tts-1` does Root cause, for whoever picks this up: the speech entrypoint takes `metadata` as a named argument, then builds the litellm params it hands to the speech-to-completion bridge from the remaining kwargs, so `metadata` arrives there as `None`. The bridge spreads those params into the inner completion call while reusing the outer request's logging object, and the completion call overwrites that shared object's `metadata` with `None`. By the time the proxy's spend callback runs it finds no key, user, or team on the request and skips the write. Debug logs show it directly: the Gemini call logs `user_api_key None, user_id None, team_id None, end_user_id None`, the OpenAI call right after it logs the hashed key ### User Flow Before a (hypothetical) fix: a developer whose app generates speech with Gemini through the gateway sees every call at $0 and their key budget never moves 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/audio/speech with `{"model": "gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts", "input": "spend tracking check", "voice": "Kore"}` using their virtual key and get 200 with `audio/wav` bytes back 2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/audio/speech with `{"model": "openai/tts-1", "input": "spend tracking check", "voice": "alloy"}` using the same key and get 200 with `audio/mpeg` bytes back 3. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs (or GET https://litellm-domain/spend/logs) and only the OpenAI request is listed, at $0.00027; the Gemini request is missing entirely 4. GET https://litellm-domain/key/info with their key shows `"spend": 0.00027`, only the OpenAI call, so a max budget on that key never trips no matter how much Gemini audio they generate After a (hypothetical) fix: both TTS calls are logged and billed to the key 1. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/audio/speech for `gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts` and get 200 with `audio/wav` bytes back 2. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/audio/speech for `openai/tts-1` and get 200 with `audio/mpeg` bytes back 3. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs lists both requests, the Gemini one with `call_type: aspeech` and non-zero spend computed from its input and audio output tokens 4. GET https://litellm-domain/key/info shows the key's `spend` as the sum of both calls, and a key max budget now trips on Gemini audio too ### Proof the bug occurs Config the proxy ran with (`GEMINI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `DATABASE_URL` set in the environment, `LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True`): ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts litellm_params: model: gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts api_key: os.environ/GEMINI_API_KEY - model_name: openai/tts-1 litellm_params: model: openai/tts-1 api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: sk-1234 ``` Version or commit: `litellm_internal_staging` at 7a5b98e6a9 (v1.98.0), booted with `python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config config.yaml --port 41873 --detailed_debug` Commands and their full output (real Gemini and OpenAI calls): ``` $ KEY=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:41873/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"key_alias":"tts-spend-repro-3"}' | jq -r .key) $ curl -s -o speech.wav -D - -X POST http://localhost:41873/v1/audio/speech -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts","input":"spend tracking check","voice":"Kore"}' | grep -i -E "^HTTP|x-litellm-call-id|content-type" HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-call-id: ab71b16a-e469-437f-8859-562e1c8cb3ef content-type: audio/wav $ ls -la speech.wav | awk '{print $5" bytes"}' 154170 bytes $ curl -s -o speech.mp3 -D - -X POST http://localhost:41873/v1/audio/speech -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"openai/tts-1","input":"spend tracking check","voice":"alloy"}' | grep -i -E "^HTTP|x-litellm-call-id|content-type" HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-litellm-call-id: 6dcf0e92-9d26-43c6-9999-ede7aaaecaf1 content-type: audio/mpeg $ sleep 15; curl -s "http://localhost:41873/spend/logs" -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" | jq -c '.[] | {request_id, model, call_type, spend}' {"request_id":"6dcf0e92-9d26-43c6-9999-ede7aaaecaf1","model":"openai/tts-1","call_type":"aspeech","spend":0.00027} $ curl -s "http://localhost:41873/key/info" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq -c '.info | {key_alias, spend}' {"key_alias":"tts-spend-repro-3","spend":0.00027} $ curl -s "http://localhost:41873/v1/model/info" -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" | jq -c '.data[] | {model_name, input_cost_per_token: .model_info.input_cost_per_token, output_cost_per_token: .model_info.output_cost_per_token}' {"model_name":"gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts","input_cost_per_token":3E-7,"output_cost_per_token":0.0000025} {"model_name":"openai/tts-1","input_cost_per_token":null,"output_cost_per_token":null} ``` So the Gemini model is priced, the call succeeded, and the spend log has only the OpenAI row. The proxy's own debug log for the two calls, in order: ``` 01:56:54 - LiteLLM Proxy:DEBUG: proxy_track_cost_callback.py:249 - user_api_key None, user_id None, team_id None, end_user_id None 01:56:56 - LiteLLM Proxy:DEBUG: proxy_track_cost_callback.py:249 - user_api_key d628805a57f5b935deab509bb849d9e7761e27681d714c191eee3336135a1f10, user_id None, team_id None, end_user_id None ``` The same happens with the master key and with the newer `gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview` (checked at #36788's head 32917b07fc) ### What a fix PR should look like - `litellm/main.py`, `speech()`: pass the named `metadata` (and the other named args the bridge needs) into `get_litellm_params(...)` so the litellm params handed to `speech_to_completion_bridge_handler.speech` carry the request metadata instead of `None`; alternatively have `litellm/endpoints/speech/speech_to_completion_bridge/transformation.py` `transform_request` read `metadata` off the logging object's existing litellm params and forward it, so the inner completion never clobbers what the outer request set - Whichever way, make sure the outer `aspeech` success handler ends up with the request's `metadata` and a non-zero `response_cost` in its kwargs, since the proxy's cost callback reads both from there - Regression test in a new `tests/test_litellm/endpoints/speech/speech_to_completion_bridge/test_handler.py` (no mapped test exists yet for the bridge; `tests/test_litellm/test_main.py` also works for the `speech()` side): call `aspeech` for a `gemini/...-tts` model with `metadata={"user_api_key": "..."}` and a mocked completion, assert the success callback's `kwargs["litellm_params"]["metadata"]` still holds `user_api_key`; a second assertion that the same holds for the OpenAI path keeps the two in lockstep - Out of scope: pricing of TTS models (already correct in `/v1/model/info`), and the `x-litellm-response-cost` header, which is empty for every `/v1/audio/speech` call and can be its own follow-up - Proof for the fix PR: the exact commands above against a live proxy at the fix commit, showing a Gemini row in `/spend/logs` with `call_type: aspeech` and non-zero `spend`, and `/key/info` `spend` equal to the sum of both calls ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? litellm_internal_staging @ 7a5b98e6a9 (v1.98.0) ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: Gemini native custom api_base sends system_instruction instead of canonical systemInstruction
signals.text: ### Description When using the native Gemini provider with a custom `api_base`, a request containing an OpenAI-style `system` message is serialized with the snake_case JSON key `system_instruction`. Some Gemini-compatible proxies parse this as a duplicate protobuf optional/oneof assignment and return HTTP 400: ```text Invalid value at 'request' (oneof), oneof field '_system_instruction' is already set. Cannot set 'system_instruction' ``` The same endpoint accepts the canonical Gemini REST JSON key `systemInstruction`. ### LiteLLM versions Reproduced with: - 1.91.0 - 1.96.2 (latest available from PyPI when tested) Python 3.13.14 on Windows. ### Minimal reproduction ```python import litellm litellm.completion( model="gemini/gemini-3.6-flash", api_base="https://<custom-gemini-base>/v1beta", api_key="<key>", messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Reply with exactly: ok"}, ], max_tokens=512, ) ``` Actual result: HTTP 400 with the protobuf oneof error above. A user-only request succeeds, so the failure is specifically triggered when LiteLLM extracts a system message. ### Request-body comparison Sending this directly to `/v1beta/models/<model>:generateContent` succeeds with HTTP 200: ```json { "systemInstruction": { "parts": [{"text": "You are a concise assistant."}] }, "contents": [ {"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "Reply with exactly: ok"}]} ] } ``` Changing only the key to snake_case reproduces HTTP 400: ```json { "system_instruction": { "parts": [{"text": "You are a concise assistant."}] }, "contents": [ {"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "Reply with exactly: ok"}]} ] } ``` ### Suspected source In `litellm/llms/vertex_ai/gemini/transformation.py`, the request transformer currently sets: ```python data["system_instruction"] = system_instructions ``` ### Expected behavior For native Gemini REST requests, serialize the system-instruction field using the canonical JSON name `systemInstruction`. This remains accepted by the Gemini REST endpoint and improves compatibility with custom native Gemini endpoints that do not safely handle the snake_case alias.

signals.title: [Bug]: MCP auto-execute (require_approval "never") hijacks client-side tool_use from agentic clients like Claude Code, breaking all non-MCP tools with "Error executing tool"
signals.text: ## What happened? A model configured with an MCP tool reference using `require_approval: "never"` (so the proxy auto-executes it server-side) is deployed behind an agentic client that sends its own tools in the same request, such as Claude Code sending Read/Bash/Edit. The auto-execute loop takes over the entire tool_use turn and tries to execute every tool_use block the model emits, including the client's own non-MCP tools. Those tools are not in the MCP server map, so the proxy raises a KeyError that gets swallowed into `Error executing tool: '<tool_name>'` and fed back to the model. The model retries, fails again, and eventually gives up. From the client's perspective all of its native tools (Read, Bash, etc.) are broken for any request routed to that model What I expected: when `require_approval: "never"` is set, the proxy should auto-execute only the MCP tools it injected. A tool_use whose name does not resolve to a known MCP server should be passed through to the client unchanged so the client can execute it locally, the way a normal tool_use turn works when no MCP tool is present ## User Flow Before a fix 1. A user creates a virtual key and a team in the LiteLLM proxy UI, then registers an HTTP MCP server (say `image_understand`) and grants the team access to it 2. The user attaches the MCP tool to a model via the model's LiteLLM Params, e.g. `{"tools": [{"type": "mcp", "server_url": "litellm_proxy/mcp/image_understand", "require_approval": "never"}]}` 3. The user points an agentic client (Claude Code) at `POST /v1/messages` on the proxy, using that model and that virtual key. The client sends its own tools (Read, Bash, Edit, ...) alongside whatever the proxy injects 4. The model decides to call Read on a local file. The proxy's auto-execute loop intercepts that tool_use, fails with `Error executing tool: 'Read'`, and returns the error text to the model instead of handing the tool_use back to the client 5. The model retries with Bash, gets `Error executing tool: 'Bash'`, and eventually stops with a message saying the tools are unavailable. The user sees tool call failures and the client's native tooling is dead for that model After a fix 1. Same setup as above: MCP server registered, team granted access, MCP tool attached to the model with `require_approval: "never"` 2. The user points Claude Code at `POST /v1/messages` with that model and key, sending its own tools 3. The model calls Read on a local file. The proxy recognizes Read is not one of its MCP tools, returns the tool_use block to the client in the response, and lets the client execute it locally 4. When the model calls the injected MCP tool (`image_understand`), the proxy auto-executes it server-side as before and feeds the result back 5. Both the client's native tools and the injected MCP tool work in the same turn ## Proof the bug occurs I verified the root cause by reading the current main branch (v1.98.0-dev.2). I was not able to capture a full Claude Code trace against my own proxy in time for this report, so the proof below is the code path plus the user-visible symptom. I can add a full end-to-end curl reproduction if the maintainers want one Config / setup: a model with an MCP tool attached via LiteLLM Params ```json {"tools": [{"type": "mcp", "server_url": "litellm_proxy/mcp/image_understand", "require_approval": "never"}]} ``` Version or commit: v1.98.0-dev.2 on main Commands and their full output The auto-execute loop in `litellm/llms/anthropic/experimental_pass_through/messages/mcp_handler.py` extracts every tool_use block without checking whether it belongs to an MCP server ``` # line 38-40 def _extract_tool_use_blocks(response): return tuple(block for block in _get_response_content(response) if block.get("type") == "tool_use") # line 139-158 (abridged) for _ in range(MAX_MCP_TOOL_USE_ITERATIONS): if _get_stop_reason(response) != "tool_use": break tool_use_blocks = _extract_tool_use_blocks(response) if not tool_use_blocks: break tool_results = await LiteLLM_Proxy_MCP_Handler._execute_tool_calls( tool_server_map=tool_server_map, tool_calls=list(tool_use_blocks), ... ) ``` `tool_server_map` is built only from the injected MCP tools (in `_process_mcp_tools_without_openai_transform`). When `_execute_tool_calls` looks up a client-side tool name that is not in that map, it throws KeyError ``` # litellm/responses/mcp/litellm_proxy_mcp_handler.py line 675 server_name = tool_server_map[tool_name] ``` That KeyError is caught by the broad except at line 891-905 and turned into the user-visible error string ``` # line 891-905 (abridged) except Exception as e: ... tool_results.append({ "tool_call_id": tool_call_id, "result": f"Error executing tool: {e}", "name": tool_name, }) ``` So a model emitting `tool_use` for `Read` produces `Error executing tool: 'Read'`, which matches what I observed in the proxy spend logs and what Claude Code surfaced as "tool call failed" The symptom from the agentic client side (Claude Code talking to the proxy over `/v1/messages`): the model attempts Read on a file that exists, gets `Error executing tool: 'Read'` back, tries Bash, gets `Error executing tool: 'Bash'`, then tells the user it cannot read files or run commands. A plain curl client that sends no tools of its own works perfectly against the same model, because then every tool_use resolves to an MCP tool. This is why the bug is specific to agentic clients that bring their own tools ## What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ## What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.98.0-dev.2 ## Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Feature]: Add Team ALIASES to /v1/models list
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### The Feature I am wanting to add models setup as aliases (Specifically under teams, but technically anywhere you can use an alias.) so that these also return under /v1/models Several tools, like open-webui use the model list to generated the acceptable list/dropdown of models to be able to use. In my case, using AWS Bedrock and Using Custom Inference profiles, I have the same model being served through different paths for billing reasons. I.E - If I am running claude-sonnet-4.5, but the model name is "Custom-Anthropic-Model-1" (RANDOM EXAMPLE) I will get errors in Claude Code, since the model name isnt recognized, it assumes its a new model and applies Adaptive reasoning, which then fails on Sonnet 4.5. To fix this, I am using the team Aliases so the teams can each use claude-sonnet-5 as the model name, and it routes to the correct inference profile for that team. (AWESOME FEATURE BTW!) However, this can get confusing for when the team or their tools hit /v1/models ### User Flow 1. User generates key 2. User looks at the model list, they see (Claude-Sonnet-Project-Name) 3. They don't realize they can use the claude-sonnet-5 alias for their team. 4. Things such as reasoning, prompt caching can break with certain tools. ### How far you got Currently, it is just providing additional user education. It is workable, but would be much cleaner if they just saw the aliases as actual models in their list ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? signals.title: [Bug]: chatgpt/* non-streaming chat completions fail with "Unknown items in responses API response: []" (streaming works)
signals.text: ## Summary For `chatgpt/*` routes using an existing valid ChatGPT OAuth `auth.json`, non-streaming chat completions regress after LiteLLM 1.88.1, while streaming continues to work. The failure is reproducible on the same route, same auth, same prompt, and same container; changing only `stream=false` to `stream=true` changes the result. ## Version matrix | LiteLLM version | `stream=false` | `stream=true` | |---|---|---| | 1.88.1 | PASS | PASS, but retry/fallback accounting headers are absent | | 1.91.0 | FAIL | PASS | | 1.96.2 | FAIL | PASS | For 1.91.0 and 1.96.2, the non-streaming failure is: ```text ChatgptException: Unknown items in responses API response: [] ``` No 401/403 or token error is observed; authentication succeeds and the provider is reached. ## Minimal reproducer Use a single model group backed by `chatgpt/gpt-5.4` with a valid OAuth `auth.json` exposed via `CHATGPT_TOKEN_DIR`, then send the same prompt twice: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: repro-chatgpt litellm_params: model: chatgpt/gpt-5.4 ``` Request 1: ```json { "model": "repro-chatgpt", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply exactly: AUTH OK"}], "stream": false, "max_tokens": 16 } ``` Request 2: identical except: ```json "stream": true ``` Observed on 1.96.2: - `stream=false`: fails with `Unknown items in responses API response: []` - `stream=true`: succeeds and returns the expected assistant content The same split reproduces with `max_tokens` 16, 128, 256, and 1024, so this does not appear to be an output-budget issue. ## Additional observations On 1.96.2, the streaming path is otherwise healthy: - incremental SSE works - usage is returned with `stream_options.include_usage` - `x-litellm-attempted-retries` is present - `x-litellm-attempted-fallbacks` is present - tool-call streaming completes successfully A controlled retry reports `x-litellm-attempted-retries: 1`, and a controlled fallback reports `x-litellm-attempted-fallbacks: 1`, so the accounting values reflect actual routing behavior. ## Suspected area The observable exception comes from the non-streaming Responses transformation path in: ```text litellm/completion_extras/litellm_responses_transformation/transformation.py ``` The relevant path converts `raw_response.output` to chat-completion choices and raises when no recognized output items can be recovered. The check itself also exists in 1.88.1, where the same request succeeds. The regression therefore appears to be that `output_items` reaches this transform empty and recovery no longer reconstructs the provider response. ### Hypothesis, not confirmed root cause The ChatGPT backend may still deliver the payload in an SSE-like form for this path, with non-streaming behavior depending on recovery from the raw/logged response. If that recovery stopped receiving or reconstructing the raw output after 1.88.1, it would explain why streaming remains healthy while non-streaming fails. This is only a hypothesis; the reproducible version split and stream/non-stream behavior above are the measured facts. ## Expected behavior The same `chatgpt/*` route and OAuth authentication should work for both streaming and non-streaming requests, as it does in LiteLLM 1.88.1.

signals.title: [Bug]: Ollama: get_runtime_model_info ignores the request's api_base and falls back to localhost:11434, adding ~8s of silent connect timeouts per completion
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? ### What happens Every `litellm.completion()` against an Ollama server on a non-default host pays **two ~4s TCP connect timeouts before the model is ever asked anything.** The failure is swallowed by a bare `except`, so it does not surface as an error — it looks like a slow model. `completion(model="ollama/...", api_base="http://my-host:30000", ...)` sends the *completion* to the right host, but the model-info lookup on the same code path resolves its own host independently: ``` litellm/main.py:5155 responses_api_bridge_check(...) -> utils.py _get_model_info_helper(...) -> ollama/common_utils.py:219 OllamaModelInfo.get_model_info(...) -> ollama/common_utils.py:170 get_runtime_model_info(model, api_base=None) ``` `get_runtime_model_info` is called without the `api_base` the caller supplied, so it falls through to the default (`common_utils.py:72`): ```python @staticmethod def get_api_base(api_base: Optional[str] = None) -> str: # env var OLLAMA_API_BASE or default return api_base or get_secret_str("OLLAMA_API_BASE") or "http://localhost:11434" ``` With nothing listening on `localhost:11434`, the POST to `/api/show` waits out the connect timeout and raises, and `common_utils.py:191` turns that into a silent default: ```python except Exception: verbose_logger.debug("OllamaError: Could not get model info.") return { ... } ``` `verbose_logger.debug` means nothing is visible at default log levels. ### Measured Ollama on `my-host:30000`; nothing on `localhost:11434`. One structured completion, instrumented by wrapping `litellm.module_level_client.post`: ``` POST http://localhost:11434/api/show -> ConnectError in 4.079s POST http://localhost:11434/api/show -> ConnectError in 4.066s POST http://my-host:30000/api/show -> 200 in 0.563s <- the real one ``` Six of those on the first call in a process, two on every call after. Per-call wall clock, mean of 5 warm reps: | | without`OLLAMA_API_BASE` | with it | | ----------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------- | | total | **10.37 s** | **1.41 s** | | ...of which generation | 2.26 s | 1.30 s | | ...of which model-info lookup | **8.11 s** | 0.10 s | The server is not slow — the same `/api/show` answers `curl` in **0.09 s**. The 8.11 s is entirely waiting on a host that is not there. ### Reproduce Any machine with Ollama on a non-default host and **nothing** on `localhost:11434`: ```python import time, litellm litellm.module_level_client.post = ( lambda _p=litellm.module_level_client.post, *a, **kw: ( print("POST", kw.get("url")), _p(*a, **kw))[1] ) began = time.perf_counter() litellm.completion( model="ollama/<your-model>", api_base="http://<your-ollama-host>:<port>", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}], ) print(f"{time.perf_counter() - began:.2f}s") ``` Expected: one POST, to your host. Actual: three, two of them to `localhost:11434`, and ~8s of the total spent failing to reach it. Setting `OLLAMA_API_BASE` to the same value as `api_base` works around it completely. ### Why this is worth fixing rather than documenting 1. **It is silent.** A bare `except` plus a `debug`-level log means the only symptom is latency, attributed to the model. It took a profiler to find — named timers around `litellm.completion` cannot see it, because it happens *inside* that call. 2. **`api_base` was supplied.** The caller did say where the server is; that value simply is not threaded to the lookup. This is not a missing configuration so much as configuration being dropped one frame down. 3. **The cost is disproportionate.** ~8s of dead time added to a ~2s generation is a 5x slowdown, and it scales with the number of calls — an agent loop making six phase calls per run pays it six times. ### The per-call path is a 4-line fix, and I have tested it Everything below `responses_api_bridge_check` already accepts and forwards `api_base` — `_get_model_info_helper` (`utils.py:5228`), `OllamaModelInfo.get_model_info` (`common_utils.py:221`) and `get_runtime_model_info` (`common_utils.py:172`) all take it. The only break is the top frame, which neither accepts it nor passes it on, even though `completion()` has it in scope at both call sites. ```diff --- a/litellm/main.py +++ b/litellm/main.py @@ def responses_api_bridge_check( def responses_api_bridge_check( model: str, custom_llm_provider: str, + api_base: Optional[str] = None, web_search_options: Optional[OpenAIWebSearchOptions] = None, tools: Optional[List[Any]] = None, @@ (inside responses_api_bridge_check) model_info = cast( dict, - _get_model_info_helper(model=model, custom_llm_provider=custom_llm_provider), + _get_model_info_helper( + model=model, + custom_llm_provider=custom_llm_provider, + api_base=api_base, + ), ) @@ main.py:5155 (completion) responses_api_model_info, model = responses_api_bridge_check( model=model, custom_llm_provider=custom_llm_provider, + api_base=api_base, web_search_options=web_search_options, ) @@ main.py:5391 (the second, later check) responses_api_model_info, model = responses_api_bridge_check( model=model, custom_llm_provider=custom_llm_provider, + api_base=api_base, web_search_options=web_search_options, ``` Backwards compatible: the new parameter is optional and keyword-only in practice, and `responses_api_bridge_check` has no callers outside `main.py`. **Measured with that patch applied and `OLLAMA_API_BASE` deliberately unset**, so only the patch can help: ``` rep 1 15.51s (4 remaining localhost timeouts — see below) rep 2 1.44s all POSTs to the configured host rep 3 1.06s all POSTs to the configured host ``` ### A second, separate path — cold start only The four timeouts left in rep 1 come from somewhere else, and they are `lru_cache`d so they only cost once per process: ``` cost_calculator.py:654 cost_per_token -> utils.py:5175 _cached_get_model_info_helper(model=..., custom_llm_provider=...) -> _get_model_info_helper -> ollama get_model_info(api_base=None) ``` `_cached_get_model_info_helper` accepts `api_base` too, but `cost_per_token` has no `api_base` in scope to give it — the cost calculator is reached from the logging layer with a response object rather than the request's kwargs. Threading it there is a real change rather than a 1-line one, which is why I have split it out. Its cost is bounded (~16s once per process, not per call), so the 4-line patch above is the part that matters for throughput. ### Suggested fixes, roughly in order of preference 1. **Thread `api_base` through** — the 4-line patch above, which covers the per-call path. Happy to open it as a PR if that is useful. 2. **Do not silently swallow a connection failure.** Even keeping the fallback dict, `verbose_logger.warning` (not `debug`) with the URL and the elapsed time would have made this self-diagnosing. 3. **Cache the lookup per `(model, api_base)`.** Two identical `/api/show` requests per completion is wasteful even when the host is right — a warm run still spends ~0.10s per completion re-fetching immutable metadata. 4. **Short-circuit the fallback host.** If `api_base` was explicitly supplied for the completion and the lookup is about to use a *different* host, that is almost certainly not intended. ### Environment - litellm 1.95.0 - instructor 1.15.4 (present, but not implicated — reproduces with plain `litellm.completion`) - Python 3.14.3, Windows - Ollama on a remote host, non-default port [issue.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31105485/issue.md) ### User Flow What happens Every litellm.completion() against an Ollama server on a non-default host pays two ~4s TCP connect timeouts before the model is ever asked anything. The failure is swallowed by a bare except, so it does not surface as an error — it looks like a slow model. ### Proof the bug occurs ### Reproduce Any machine with Ollama on a non-default host and nothing on localhost:11434 ``` import time, litellm litellm.module_level_client.post = ( lambda _p=litellm.module_level_client.post, *a, **kw: ( print("POST", kw.get("url")), _p(*a, **kw))[1] ) began = time.perf_counter() litellm.completion( model="ollama/<your-model>", api_base="http://<your-ollama-host>:<port>", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}], ) print(f"{time.perf_counter() - began:.2f}s") ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? SDK (litellm Python package) ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? litellm 1.95.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_
signals.author: benoitf73

signals.title: [Bug]: service_tier=priority silently billed at default rate for gpt-4o/gpt-4.1 family (missing pricing keys on dated-snapshot model entries)
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? ## Actual behaviour For `gpt-4o`, `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4.1`, and `gpt-4.1-mini`, sending `service_tier="priority"` is accepted by OpenAI (the response correctly echoes back `response.service_tier == "priority"`), but the cost LiteLLM computes (`x-litellm-response-cost` header / spend logs) is identical to the **default**-tier cost, not the priority-tier cost. By contrast, the same test against `gpt-5`, `gpt-5-mini`, `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.4-mini` correctly applies priority/flex pricing. ## Live verification (thunk-prod proxy, tiny `max_tokens=5` calls) | model | tier | prompt/completion tokens | reported cost | expected cost (priority rate) | |---|---|---|---|---| | gpt-4o-mini | priority | 9 / 2 | 2.55e-06 | 4.25e-06 | | gpt-4o | priority | 9 / 1 | 3.25e-05 | 5.525e-05 | | gpt-4.1 | priority | 9 / 1 | 2.6e-05 | 4.55e-05 | | gpt-4.1-mini | priority | 9 / 1 | 5.2e-06 | 9.1e-06 | In every case the "reported cost" exactly matches what default-tier pricing would produce for the same token counts, confirming priority pricing was silently not applied. ## Root cause `model_prices_and_context_window_backup.json` defines `input_cost_per_token_priority` / `output_cost_per_token_priority` on the **alias** entries (`gpt-4o`, `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4.1`, `gpt-4.1-mini`) but **not** on the **dated-snapshot** entries that OpenAI actually echoes back in `response.model` (`gpt-4o-2024-08-06`, `gpt-4o-2024-11-20`, `gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18`, `gpt-4.1-2025-04-14`, `gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14`): ``` gpt-4o priority_in=4.25e-06 priority_out=1.7e-05 gpt-4o-2024-08-06 priority_in=None priority_out=None gpt-4o-2024-11-20 priority_in=None priority_out=None gpt-4o-mini priority_in=2.5e-07 priority_out=1e-06 gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 priority_in=None priority_out=None gpt-4.1 priority_in=3.5e-06 priority_out=1.4e-05 gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 priority_in=None priority_out=None gpt-4.1-mini priority_in=7e-07 priority_out=2.8e-06 gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 priority_in=None priority_out=None ``` `cost_calculator.py`'s model-name resolution (`_select_model_name_for_cost_calc` / `potential_model_names`, around lines 688-692 and 1115-1131) prefers the dated snapshot name echoed by OpenAI over the caller-supplied alias when looking up pricing. `litellm_core_utils/llm_cost_calc/utils.py`'s `_get_cost_per_unit` (~lines 349-388) then silently falls back to base (non-priority) pricing when the `_priority` key is absent on the resolved (dated-snapshot) model_info entry — no error or warning is raised. For `gpt-5`/`gpt-5-mini`, both the alias **and** the dated-snapshot entry (`gpt-5-2025-08-07`, `gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07`) carry `_priority` keys, so the same lookup path resolves correctly there — confirming this is a pricing-data completeness gap, not a code-path difference between model families. ## Expected behaviour Priority-tier cost should be applied whenever the model actually served the request at `priority` tier, regardless of whether the model resolves via alias or dated-snapshot name. Either: 1. Add `input_cost_per_token_priority`/`output_cost_per_token_priority` (and `_flex` where applicable) to the dated-snapshot JSON entries for these models, or 2. Make the cost-key fallback in `llm_cost_calc/utils.py` fall back from a dated-snapshot entry to its alias entry (not straight to base pricing) when a tier-specific key is missing. ## Impact Any proxy user billing `service_tier=priority` traffic on `gpt-4o`, `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4.1`, or `gpt-4.1-mini` is under-reporting spend — potentially significantly, since priority pricing is ~1.7-2x the default rate on these models while actual OpenAI billing is presumably at the priority rate. ### Relevant log output _N/A — reproducible via `x-litellm-response-cost` response header, see table above._ ### Are you a ML Ops Team? - [ ] Yes ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? Reproduced against a production proxy; latest `main` as of 2026-08-15 has the same gap in `model_prices_and_context_window_backup.json`. ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: Security: budget bypass — key owner raises own max_budget via temp_budget_increase on /key/update
signals.text: ## Security: non-admin key owner raises own `max_budget` via `temp_budget_increase` on `/key/update` **Severity:** Medium (CWE-863 / CWE-770) From a read-only security survey of master @ 7a5b98e6 (2026-08-15). ### Finding `LiteLLM_ManagementEndpoint_MetadataFields` (`litellm/proxy/_types.py:4203-4204`) includes `temp_budget_increase`/`temp_budget_expiry` with **no premium/role gate**. `prepare_metadata_fields()` (`key_management_endpoints.py:1966-1987`) copies `temp_budget_*` into the key's metadata with no admin check, and `_validate_update_key_data()` does not classify these as a budget change (`_is_budget_change` only covers `max_budget`/`spend`/`budget_limits`), so a key owner (or team admin) satisfies `can_skip_admin_check=True` and skips `_check_key_admin_access`. At request time `_get_temp_budget_increase()`/`_update_key_budget_with_temp_budget_increase()` (`auth/user_api_key_auth.py:2804-2823`) adds the stored value to the token's `max_budget` while the expiry is in the future — with no positivity/size limit. ### Impact Any INTERNAL_USER with a personal virtual key can raise their own budget cap arbitrarily, defeating key/team/org budget and spend controls. ### Repro sketch `POST /key/update {"key":"<own key>","temp_budget_increase":1000000000,"temp_budget_expiry":"2099-01-01T00:00:00Z"}` → subsequent calls authenticate with `max_budget` inflated by 1e9. ### Suggested fix - Treat `temp_budget_increase`/`temp_budget_expiry` as budget changes (admin-gated), and validate/limit the increase value.
signals.author: krow-with-lonel

signals.title: Security: SSRF / provider-key exfiltration via client-supplied api_base (validate guard is dead code)
signals.text: ## Security: SSRF / provider-key exfiltration via client-supplied `api_base` under clientside-auth opt-ins (guard is dead code) **Severity:** Medium (CWE-918 / CWE-522) From a read-only security survey of master @ 7a5b98e6 (2026-08-15). ### Finding The proxy-wide ban on client-supplied `api_base`/`base_url` (`proxy/auth/auth_utils.py` `_BANNED_REQUEST_BODY_PARAMS`) is lifted by two documented opt-ins: `general_settings.allow_client_side_credentials=true` and per-deployment `configurable_clientside_auth_params: [api_base]`. When either is set, `_check_banned_params` (`auth_utils.py:319-377`) skips the rejection and **no URL validation runs anywhere on that value**: the intended guard `check_complete_credentials` (`auth_utils.py:65-112`, which calls `validate_url`) has **no production callers** (dead code — only unit tests reference it), and the outbound provider POST (`llms/custom_httpx/llm_http_handler.py:275-280`, `aiohttp_handler.py:173-178`) posts straight to the client-chosen `api_base` with the deployment's `api_key` in the Authorization header. ### Impact A caller with access to such a model group can point the proxy at internal/cloud-metadata hosts (SSRF) or at an attacker host to harvest the deployment's provider API key. ### Repro sketch With a deployment configured `configurable_clientside_auth_params: ["api_base"]`: `POST /v1/chat/completions {"model":"<that-model>","api_base":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/","messages":[...]}` → proxy fetches internal content; or `api_base` = attacker host → provider key arrives in the request. ### Suggested fix - Wire `check_complete_credentials`/`validate_url` into the request path for any client-supplied `api_base` (or remove the dead code and add the check where the value is consumed).
signals.author: krow-with-lonel

signals.title: Security: no-auth mode when LITELLM_MASTER_KEY unset (default docker-compose does not set it)
signals.text: ## Security: proxy runs with no authentication when `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` is unset; shipped docker-compose default does not set it **Severity:** Low (CWE-306 / CWE-287) From a read-only security survey of master @ 7a5b98e6 (2026-08-15). ### Finding When `master_key` is None and JWT/OAuth2 auth is not configured, `_user_api_key_auth_builder` (`proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py:1476-1487`) returns an INTERNAL_USER token for ANY `api_key` value (even garbage), and `_authorize_authenticated_request` (`:2217-2230`) skips authz entirely ("No-auth dev mode"). The default `docker-compose.yml` (`:10-28`) does not set `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` (it only reads an optional `.env`), so a fresh `docker compose up` following the quickstart leaves all inference routes open to anyone who can reach port 4000, using the operator's configured upstream credentials. ### Impact Cost abuse, quota exhaustion, DoS — free inference via the operator's paid upstream. Startup logs a CRITICAL warning, but the default compose makes this the default configuration. ### Suggested fix - Set a generated `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` in the shipped docker-compose (or fail startup when unset in non-dev mode).

signals.title: fix(http_handler): bypass cache when shared_session is provided for aiohttp tracing
signals.text: ## Description Fixes #20174 - aiohttp client tracing logs not visible when using LiteLLM. ### Problem When users pass a `shared_session` with `trace_configs` to `acompletion()`, the `get_async_httpx_client()` function was ignoring the user's session and returning a cached client. This meant the user's tracing configuration was never used, so aiohttp tracing logs were never emitted. ### Root Cause In `get_async_httpx_client()`: ```python _cached_client = cache.get_cache(_cache_key_name) if _cached_client: return _cached_client # <-- User's shared_session is completely ignored! ``` The cache lookup happened before checking if `shared_session` was provided, so any cached client for that provider was returned, ignoring the user's custom session configuration. ### Solution When `shared_session` is provided, bypass the cache entirely and create a new handler that uses the user's session directly. This preserves the user's `ClientSession` configuration including: - `trace_configs` (for aiohttp tracing) - Custom connector settings - Any other session-level configuration ### Test Plan - Added `test_shared_session_bypasses_cache` - verifies cache is bypassed when `shared_session` is provided - Added `test_shared_session_each_call_gets_new_handler` - verifies each call with a different `shared_session` gets its own handler - All existing tests continue to pass (34 tests in test_http_handler.py)

signals.title: feat(openrouter): add image edit support for OpenRouter models
signals.text: ## Relevant issues Fixes https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/22305 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have Added testing in the [`tests/litellm/`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/tree/main/tests/litellm) directory, **Adding at least 1 test is a hard requirement** - [see details](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/extras/contributing_code) - [x] My PR passes all unit tests on [`make test-unit`](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/extras/contributing_code) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible, it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have requested a Greptile review by commenting `@greptileai` and received a **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Type New Feature ## Changes ### Problem OpenRouter models (e.g., `google/gemini-2.5-flash-image`) support image editing through their chat completions endpoint, but LiteLLM has no image edit configuration for the OpenRouter provider. Calling `litellm.image_edit()` with an OpenRouter model raises `ValueError("image edit is not supported for openrouter")` because `ProviderConfigManager.get_provider_image_edit_config()` returns `None` for OpenRouter. ### Solution Added `OpenRouterImageEditConfig` that implements `BaseImageEditConfig` to route image edit requests through OpenRouter's chat completions endpoint. Unlike providers with dedicated `/images/edits` endpoints, OpenRouter handles image editing via `/api/v1/chat/completions` with the source image sent as a base64 data URL in the message content and `modalities: ["image", "text"]` to signal image output. - Converts source images (bytes, BytesIO, BufferedReader) to base64 data URLs in the messages array - Maps OpenAI parameters: `size` to `image_config.aspect_ratio`, `quality` to `image_config.image_size` - Parses edited images from `choices[].message.images[]` in the response - Tracks usage including input image tokens from `prompt_tokens_details` - Extracts cost and cost details from OpenRouter's usage response - Uses JSON requests (`use_multipart_form_data() = False`), matching the Gemini image edit pattern - Registered in `ProviderConfigManager.get_provider_image_edit_config()` following the existing factory pattern ### Files changed - **`litellm/llms/openrouter/image_edit/__init__.py`** - New module with factory function `get_openrouter_image_edit_config()` - **`litellm/llms/openrouter/image_edit/transformation.py`** - `OpenRouterImageEditConfig` class with request/response transformation, parameter mapping, usage/cost extraction - **`litellm/utils.py`** - Added OpenRouter case to `ProviderConfigManager.get_provider_image_edit_config()` - **`tests/test_litellm/llms/openrouter/image_edit/__init__.py`** - Test module init - **`tests/test_litellm/llms/openrouter/image_edit/test_openrouter_image_edit_transformation.py`** - 33 unit tests ### Testing - 33 new unit tests covering: supported params, multipart mode, parameter mapping (size, quality, n, combined, unknown), size-to-aspect-ratio mapping, quality-to-image-size mapping, URL construction, environment validation, request transformation (basic, BytesIO, multiple images, optional params, base64 encoding, no prompt), response transformation (base64, URL, usage/cost, multiple images, JSON error), error class, and `_read_image_bytes` edge cases - All 33 new tests pass - All 48 existing OpenRouter tests continue to pass (81 total) - Live-tested against the OpenRouter API with `google/gemini-2.5-flash-image`, successfully editing an image and receiving a valid response with correct usage tracking @greptileai @shin-bot-litellm

signals.title: fix(snowflake): transform string tool_choice to object format
signals.text: ## Summary Fixes #23284 Snowflake's Cortex LLM API (like Anthropic's Messages API) requires `tool_choice` as an object with a `"type"` field, not as a bare string. Passing `tool_choice="auto"` (or `"required"`/`"none"`) results in Snowflake error 390142 "invalid payload". ### Root cause The `_transform_tool_choice` method in `SnowflakeConfig` was passing string `tool_choice` values through unchanged. However, Snowflake's API follows the Anthropic convention where `tool_choice` must be an object like `{"type": "auto"}`. LiteLLM's own Anthropic handler (`AnthropicConfig._map_tool_choice`) already correctly transforms strings to objects -- the Snowflake handler was missing the same transformation. ### Fix Transform OpenAI string `tool_choice` values to Snowflake's object format: | OpenAI (string) | Snowflake (object) | |---|---| | `"auto"` | `{"type": "auto"}` | | `"required"` | `{"type": "any"}` | | `"none"` | `{"type": "none"}` | The `"required"` -> `"any"` mapping follows the same convention used by Anthropic/Snowflake (the model must use at least one tool). The existing dict-to-dict transformation for specific function tool choices remains unchanged. ### Tests updated Updated `test_transform_request_with_string_tool_choice` to verify the new object format output instead of passthrough. ## Test plan - [ ] Verify `tool_choice="auto"` is transformed to `{"type": "auto"}` - [ ] Verify `tool_choice="required"` is transformed to `{"type": "any"}` - [ ] Verify `tool_choice="none"` is transformed to `{"type": "none"}` - [ ] Verify dict tool_choice (specific function) still works - [ ] Verify requests without tool_choice are unaffected
